title: Practice Passage 18: The Mechanics of Volcanic Eruptions

passage.title: The Mechanics of Volcanic Eruptions
passage.sub_title: Understanding magma chambers, central conduits, horizontal sills, vertical dikes, side vents, and explosive ash clouds.
passage.content_html:
Paragraph A

[A1] Volcanic eruptions are among the most powerful geological forces on Earth. [A2] They occur when molten rock, known as magma, rises from deep within the Earth's mantle to the surface. [A3] As magma ascends, it accumulates in a large underground chamber located beneath the volcano. [A4] This chamber acts as a storage reservoir, where intense heat and pressure build up over thousands of years.

Paragraph B

[B1] The structural anatomy of a volcano dictates how magma travels to the surface. [B2] The main vertical path is the central vent, also called the conduit. [B3] This main conduit connects the deep magma chamber directly to the primary opening at the peak of the volcano, known as the crater. [B4] Eruptions typically eject ash, gas, and lava through this primary crater.

Paragraph C

[C1] However, magma does not always follow the central pathway. [C2] In many volcanoes, high pressure forces magma through cracks in the surrounding rock, forming secondary paths. [C3] A side vent is a secondary passage that branches off from the central conduit and opens on the flank of the volcano. [C4] Eruptions from these side vents can create smaller, secondary cones on the volcanic slopes.

Paragraph D

[D1] Magma that cools and solidifies within horizontal cracks forms geological structures called sills. [D2] A sill is a horizontal sheet of volcanic rock that squeezes between existing layers of sedimentary rock. [D3] In contrast, magma that forces its way vertically through surrounding rock layers forms structures known as dikes. [D4] Dikes act as vertical walls of igneous rock that cut across horizontal rock strata.

Paragraph E

[E1] During an explosive eruption, the composition of the ejected material changes rapidly. [E2] As gas-rich magma reaches the low pressure of the surface, dissolved gases expand violently. [E3] This expansion shatters the molten rock into tiny particles of ash, creating a massive ash cloud that rises into the atmosphere. [E4] These towering ash clouds can block sunlight and disrupt global air travel.

Paragraph F

[F1] Lava flow is another major product of volcanic eruptions. [F2] Once magma reaches the surface, it is referred to as lava. [F3] The viscosity, or thickness, of the lava determines how fast and far it flows. [F4] Runny, low-viscosity lava creates wide, flat flows, whereas thick, high-viscosity lava builds steep volcanic domes.

Paragraph G

[G1] Volcanoes are monitored carefully by geologists to predict eruptions. [G2] Scientists use seismographs to detect small earthquakes caused by magma moving underground. [G3] Tiltmeters are also used to measure slight changes in the slope of the volcano as pressure builds. [G4] Monitoring these geological signs helps save lives by allowing authorities to issue timely evacuation orders.
